::: {.lead-note}

Indonesian public procurement generates an enormous amount of regulation and
very little written reflection on practice. These essays are an attempt to close
part of that gap: short pieces on how procurement decisions are actually made,
why they go wrong, and what the profession should be arguing about.

:::

::: {.note}

Essays are in preparation. The pieces below are the ones I intend to write
first; each will be published here as it is finished.

:::

## In preparation

::: {.insight-item}

### Beyond the Lowest Price: What "Value" Means in Public Procurement
Why the lowest evaluated bid is a decision rule rather than an outcome, and what
a public buyer gives up when price is the only dimension that is scored.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### Procurement Strategy Is Decided Before the Tender Opens
Packaging, market approach, and contract type determine the range of achievable
outcomes. By the time the tender is announced, most of the value has already
been won or lost.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### Managing Contract Performance, Not Contract Documents
Indonesian procurement practice is strong on document compliance and weak on
performance management. What changes when the contract is treated as a
management instrument rather than a legal artefact.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### Rethinking the Kraljic Matrix for Government Procurement
A portfolio model built for private manufacturing is widely taught to public
buyers. Where it transfers, where it misleads, and what a public-sector
equivalent would need to account for.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### From Procurement Dashboards to an End-to-End Procurement Pipeline
Indonesia has invested heavily in procurement data collection. The remaining
problem is that the data are reported rather than used. What an integrated
procurement pipeline would have to look like.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Public Procurement
Which parts of the procurement cycle are genuinely automatable, which are
judgement calls that should stay with accountable officials, and what the
distinction implies for how procurement officers are trained.

:::
